Let $M$ be a smooth Hausdorff second-countable manifold **without boundary**, in the sense of [[def-smooth-manifold]]. Let $g$ be a positive definite smooth Riemannian metric as in [[def-riemannian-metric-symmetric-cotangent-connection-and-covariant-hessian]]. Use the Levi-Civita connection of [[def-levi-civita-connection]] with the existence and coordinate formula supplied by [[prop-christoffel-formula-for-the-levi-civita-connection]]; in coordinates it has coefficients $\Gamma^k_{ij}=\frac12g^{kl}(\partial_i g_{jl}+\partial_j g_{il}-\partial_l g_{ij})$. A parametrized affine geodesic is a smooth curve $\gamma:J\to M$ on an interval with nonempty interior satisfying $\nabla_{\dot\gamma}\dot\gamma=0$, equivalently $\ddot\gamma^k+\Gamma^k_{ij}(\gamma)\dot\gamma^i\dot\gamma^j=0$, where covariant differentiation along the curve is defined by [[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]; the coordinate equation is the expansion of that derivative in a coordinate basis. Its maximal domain is an interval on which it cannot be extended with the same affine parameter as a solution. **Two-sided geodesic completeness** means that every maximal affine geodesic is defined on all of $\mathbb R$.

Independently, for a real metric $d$ in [[def-metric-space]], a sequence $(x_n)$ is Cauchy when for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $N$ with $d(x_m,x_n)<\varepsilon$ whenever $m,n\ge N$. It converges to $x$ when for every $\varepsilon>0$ eventually $d(x_n,x)<\varepsilon$. **Metric completeness** means that every Cauchy sequence converges in the given metric space. In a Riemannian application the metric must be the distance induced by $g$ on a connected component: the infimum of lengths $\int\sqrt{g(\dot\alpha,\dot\alpha)}\,dt$ over piecewise-$C^1$ connecting curves. Its definition and finite metric property are supplied by [[def-riemannian-distance-on-a-connected-manifold]] and [[thm-riemannian-distance-is-a-metric]]. Specify that induced metric, rather than an arbitrary compatible metric. Distinct components are treated separately; no infinite distance is inserted into a real metric.

These are different completeness conditions. Their equivalence is a Hopf–Rinow theorem requiring its own hypotheses and proof; it is not part of this definition. In particular, a Lorentzian metric is not a positive definite distance, and this convention supplies no Lorentzian Hopf–Rinow implication.

The boundaryless restriction matters: the Euclidean interval $[0,1]$ is metrically complete, while the curve $\gamma(t)=1/2+t$ stays inside it only for $-1/2\le t\le1/2$ and cannot be continued there as a two-sided affine geodesic with velocity $1$. Completeness of this interval follows because a real Cauchy sequence converges in $\mathbb R$ by [[thm-reals-cauchy-complete]] and its limit remains between $0$ and $1$. This boundary example explains the domain restriction; it is not an instance of the boundaryless equivalence.

It is not a new set or a domain for unrestricted quantification. Work with the usual set axioms, in particular [[def-axiom-of-power-set]] and [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]], and the ordered pairs, products and functions of [[def-ordered-pair]], [[def-cartesian-product]] and [[def-function]]. The power-set axiom supplies a collecting set; Separation trims it to exactly $\mathcal P(X)=\{Y:Y\subseteq X\}$.

A **small category** has a set $O$ of objects, a set $A$ of arrows, source and target functions $s,t:A\to O$, an identity function $e:O\to A$, and a composition function on the set $\{(a,b)\in A\times A:s(a)=t(b)\}$, where $ab$ denotes $a\circ b$ and the laws are $s(e(x))=t(e(x))=x$, $s(ab)=s(b)$, $t(ab)=t(a)$, $e(t(a))a=a=ae(s(a))$, and $(ab)c=a(bc)$ whenever the displayed compositions are defined. It is **locally small** when each specified hom-collection is a set. A definable large category is a schema of formulas for its objects, arrows and operations, with those laws asserted as formulas; it is not a set of all objects or a category of all large categories. No Grothendieck universe is assumed.

All indexed families in the local bundle construction have a supplied set index $I$. If $U_i\subseteq M$ and $G$ is a set, their tagged disjoint union is the subset $D=\{(i,x,z)\in I\times M\times G:x\in U_i\}$, formed by Separation. Given a set equivalence relation $E\subseteq D\times D$, each class $[u]_E=\{v\in D:(u,v)\in E\}$ is a subset of $D$, and the quotient is the set

$$
D/E=\{C\in\mathcal P(D):\exists u\in D\ \forall v\in D\ (v\in C\iff(u,v)\in E)\}.
$$

Thus the quotient is obtained by Separation in $\mathcal P(D)$, without choosing representatives. Transition-map graphs and connection data are subsets of specified finite products and power sets, not arbitrary proper-class objects.

For the Cauchy-development coding application, fix a set manifold $\Sigma$ and the tensor-bundle total spaces over $\Sigma\times\mathbb R$. A code consists of an open set $D\subseteq\Sigma\times\mathbb R$, graphs of a metric and a two-form on $D$ inside those fixed total spaces, a time orientation, and a fixed initial embedding. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth, Hausdorff, second-countable four-manifold without boundary, with smooth Lorentzian metric $g$ of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and smooth time-orientation field $N$, as in [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]. Supply an independent orientation $o$ of $M$ in the sense of [[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. The metric and time orientation do not select $o$. Write $\mathrm{vol}_g$ for the oriented metric volume form of [[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]]; in any positively oriented chart it has components $\sqrt{|\det(g_{ab})|}\,dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$.

A smooth real $k$-form is a smooth section of $\bigwedge^kT^*M$, and its space is denoted $\Omega^k(M)$, as in [[def-smooth-differential-k-form]]. In this page, $F\in\Omega^2(M)$ means an arbitrary smooth real two-form. No equation such as $dF=0$, no global potential, and no physical field law is included in this definition.

An **observer at $p\in M$** is a vector $n\in T_pM$ with $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and $g_p(n,N_p)<0$; its **rest space** is $n^\perp=\{v:g_p(v,n)=0\}$, as in [[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]. A smooth **observer congruence** on an open set $U\subseteq M$ is a smooth vector field whose value at every point is an observer. Its observer curves are the maximal integral curves, and a chart is adapted to it when its three spatial coordinate functions are constant along those curves, as in [[def-gr-observer-congruence-and-adapted-charts]]. Such a congruence need not be hypersurface-orthogonal.

A **local frame field** on $U$ is an ordered smooth basis field of $TM|_U$. A **coordinate frame** is the basis of coordinate vector fields supplied by a chart. A **tetrad field** is a local frame $(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ with $g(E_A,E_B)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{AB}$; it is future-directed when $E_0$ is future-directed, as in [[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]]. These are distinct objects: an observer congruence is a vector field, an adapted chart is a coordinate chart, and a tetrad is a basis field. A tetrad field is not presumed to be a coordinate frame. For every observer congruence $n$, each point has a neighborhood carrying an $n$-adapted tetrad; this is a local assertion only.

A **worldline** on this Lorentzian manifold means a $C^1$ or piecewise-$C^1$ regular curve with future-timelike tangent and specified interval domain, as defined precisely in [[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]. Its parameter is arbitrary; the proper-time and four-velocity constructions of that definition apply under their stated hypotheses. A worldline is a mathematical curve here and does not assert the existence or motion of a physical body.

For coordinate bookkeeping only, when a chart is chosen with all four coordinate values assigned the metre, write $x^0=ct$, where $t$ is assigned seconds and $c>0$ is the corresponding scale in $\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}$. Then $g_{ab}$ is recorded as dimensionless. This is a unit convention on a chart, not a claim that the chart is inertial, orthonormal, global, or physically realized; $c$ in this mathematical convention has no asserted measured value.

Use the unique torsion-free metric-compatible connection $\nabla^g$ and the curvature convention of [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]] and [[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]]. In a length-coordinate chart, the displayed Christoffel formula differentiates dimensionless metric components once, so $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ is recorded in $\mathrm m^{-1}$. The curvature coordinate formula contains one derivative of $\Gamma$ or a product of two $\Gamma$ components, so $R^a{}_{bcd}$ and its Ricci and scalar contractions are recorded in $\mathrm m^{-2}$. These component assignments apply only in length-coordinate charts; other coordinate units transform by their Jacobians.

Let $(M,g,N,o)$ have the oriented, time-oriented Lorentzian structure and volume form of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]]. On decomposable $k$-covectors define the induced exterior pairing by

$$\langle\alpha_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\alpha_k,\beta_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\beta_k\rangle_g:=\det\bigl(g^{-1}(\alpha_i,\beta_j)\bigr),$$

and extend it bilinearly. For $0\le k\le4$, its coordinate expression is the pointwise exterior metric on $k$-covectors

$$\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_g:=\frac1{k!}\alpha_{a_1\cdots a_k}\beta^{a_1\cdots a_k},$$

where indices are raised by $g^{-1}$. There is a unique smooth bundle map $\star_g:\Omega^k(M)\to\Omega^{4-k}(M)$ characterized by

$$\alpha\wedge\star_g\beta=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_g\,\mathrm{vol}_g$$

at every point. In a positively oriented $g$-orthonormal coframe $(e^0,e^1,e^2,e^3)$, put $\epsilon_0=-1$ and $\epsilon_1=\epsilon_2=\epsilon_3=1$. For an increasing index set $I\subseteq\{0,1,2,3\}$, let $I^c$ be its increasing complement, let $s(I,I^c)$ be the sign of the permutation $(I,I^c)$ to $(0,1,2,3)$, and set $\epsilon_I:=\prod_{i\in I}\epsilon_i$. Then

$$\star_g e^I=\epsilon_I s(I,I^c)e^{I^c}.$$

Consequently, on $k$-forms,

$$\star_g^2=(-1)^{k(4-k)+1}\operatorname{id}.$$

In particular $\star_g^2=-\operatorname{id}$ on two-forms. For a two-form $F$, the component formula in a positively oriented chart is

$$({\star_gF})_{ab}=\frac12(\mathrm{vol}_g)_{abcd}F^{cd}.$$

The exterior derivative in [[def-exterior-derivative-by-the-invariant-vector-field-formula]] has the local coordinate formula of [[thm-local-coordinate-formula-for-the-exterior-derivative]], satisfies $d^2=0$, and obeys the graded product rule of [[thm-the-exterior-derivative-is-a-graded-derivation]].

Let $a<b$ and $c<d$. Suppose $g,h:[a,b]\times[c,d]\to\mathbb R$ are continuous and, for every fixed $t\in[c,d]$, the function $x\mapsto g(x,t)$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$ with derivative $h(x,t)$. Define

$$G(x):=\int_c^d g(x,t)\,dt.$$

Then $G$ is differentiable on $[a,b]$ as a function on that interval and

$$G'(x)=\int_c^d h(x,t)\,dt\qquad(x\in[a,b]).$$

At $a$ and $b$ the derivative is relative and one-sided. The derivative hypothesis is imposed only for interior parameter values; continuity of $h$ supplies its endpoint values.

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

derivations.claim: Put $y=x-p$. Fix $x_0\in D$ and choose a closed coordinate box $K\subset D$ with $x_0$ in its interior. The image of $K\times[0,1]$ under $(x,t)\mapsto p+t(x-p)$ is compact and lies in $D$, so the integrand $G_b(x,t)=t(x-p)^aF_{ab}(p+t(x-p))$ and every $x$-partial derivative are continuous on $K\times[0,1]$. Fixing all but one coordinate, [F3] passes that parameter derivative through the integral on the corresponding compact rectangle; applying it repeatedly to each derivative shows that every partial derivative of $A_b$ exists and is continuous near $x_0$. Since $x_0$ was arbitrary, $A_b$ is smooth on $D$, and $A=A_b\,dx^b$ is a smooth one-form.

By the differentiation-under-the-integral justification in step 1.1, differentiate the integral and use antisymmetry to obtain $\partial_cA_b-\partial_bA_c=\int_0^1\left(2tF_{cb}(p+ty)+t^2y^a(\partial_cF_{ab}-\partial_bF_{ac})(p+ty)\right)dt$. The closure identity in [F2] gives $\partial_cF_{ab}-\partial_bF_{ac}=\partial_aF_{cb}$. Thus the integrand is $\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(t^2F_{cb}(p+ty)\bigr)$.

The function $t\mapsto t^2F_{cb}(p+ty)$ is continuous on $[0,1]$, differentiable on $(0,1)$, and its derivative extends continuously to both endpoints, hence is integrable by [F5]. The Newton–Leibniz formula [F4] evaluates the integral as $F_{cb}(x)-0$, since $t^2F_{cb}(p+ty)=0$ at $t=0$. Therefore every coefficient of $dA$ equals the corresponding coefficient of $F$, so $dA=F$.

For the one-form formula, [F3] applies to the smooth integrand on the same compact-image rectangles as in step 1.1, so $\chi$ is smooth. Closedness gives $\partial_b\alpha_a=\partial_a\alpha_b$, and hence $\partial_b\chi=\int_0^1\left(\alpha_b(p+ty)+t y^a\partial_a\alpha_b(p+ty)\right)dt=\int_0^1\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(t\alpha_b(p+ty)\bigr)dt=\alpha_b(x)$ by [F4] and [F5]; the lower endpoint vanishes. Thus $d\chi=\alpha$, proving this local gauge-difference assertion without assuming a global real phase.

For $a>0$, integer $m$ and integer $n\ge1$, define the rational regime by

$$
a^{m/n}:=(a^{1/n})^m,
$$

where $a^{1/n}$ is the unique positive root of $s^n=a$ in [[thm-nth-roots-exist]], and integer powers include reciprocals for negative $m$. This is [[def-rational-power]]; [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]] proves independence of the fraction representative and [[lem-rational-power-laws]] gives the rational exponent laws. The supplementary convention is $0^r=0$ for rational $r>0$; $0^0$ and negative powers of zero remain undefined.

The separate real regime is [[def-real-power]]: for $a>0$ and $x\in\mathbb R$, $a^x=\exp(x\log a)$, with the laws of [[thm-real-power-laws]]. For $x>0$ set $0^x=0$; no arbitrary real power is assigned to a negative base. The real-power laws are supplied by that theorem, not inferred from the rational root formula. Use the real-number structure of [[def-real-numbers]].

In particular $s(q)=q^{1/2}$ for $q>0$ is the unique positive solution of $s(q)^2=q$. Its smoothness and derivative are a separate well-definedness result, not an assumption about fractional notation.

Let $M$ be a smooth Hausdorff second-countable manifold **without boundary**, in the sense of [[def-smooth-manifold]]. Let $g$ be a positive definite smooth Riemannian metric as in [[def-riemannian-metric-symmetric-cotangent-connection-and-covariant-hessian]]. Use the Levi-Civita connection of [[def-levi-civita-connection]] with the existence and coordinate formula supplied by [[prop-christoffel-formula-for-the-levi-civita-connection]]; in coordinates it has coefficients $\Gamma^k_{ij}=\frac12g^{kl}(\partial_i g_{jl}+\partial_j g_{il}-\partial_l g_{ij})$. A parametrized affine geodesic is a smooth curve $\gamma:J\to M$ on an interval with nonempty interior satisfying $\nabla_{\dot\gamma}\dot\gamma=0$, equivalently $\ddot\gamma^k+\Gamma^k_{ij}(\gamma)\dot\gamma^i\dot\gamma^j=0$, where covariant differentiation along the curve is defined by [[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]; the coordinate equation is the expansion of that derivative in a coordinate basis. Its maximal domain is an interval on which it cannot be extended with the same affine parameter as a solution. **Two-sided geodesic completeness** means that every maximal affine geodesic is defined on all of $\mathbb R$.

Independently, for a real metric $d$ in [[def-metric-space]], a sequence $(x_n)$ is Cauchy when for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $N$ with $d(x_m,x_n)<\varepsilon$ whenever $m,n\ge N$. It converges to $x$ when for every $\varepsilon>0$ eventually $d(x_n,x)<\varepsilon$. **Metric completeness** means that every Cauchy sequence converges in the given metric space. In a Riemannian application the metric must be the distance induced by $g$ on a connected component: the infimum of lengths $\int\sqrt{g(\dot\alpha,\dot\alpha)}\,dt$ over piecewise-$C^1$ connecting curves. Its definition and finite metric property are supplied by [[def-riemannian-distance-on-a-connected-manifold]] and [[thm-riemannian-distance-is-a-metric]]. Specify that induced metric, rather than an arbitrary compatible metric. Distinct components are treated separately; no infinite distance is inserted into a real metric.

These are different completeness conditions. Their equivalence is a Hopf–Rinow theorem requiring its own hypotheses and proof; it is not part of this definition. In particular, a Lorentzian metric is not a positive definite distance, and this convention supplies no Lorentzian Hopf–Rinow implication.

The boundaryless restriction matters: the Euclidean interval $[0,1]$ is metrically complete, while the curve $\gamma(t)=1/2+t$ stays inside it only for $-1/2\le t\le1/2$ and cannot be continued there as a two-sided affine geodesic with velocity $1$. Completeness of this interval follows because a real Cauchy sequence converges in $\mathbb R$ by [[thm-reals-cauchy-complete]] and its limit remains between $0$ and $1$. This boundary example explains the domain restriction; it is not an instance of the boundaryless equivalence.

Let $(M,g,N,o)$ be the smooth, Hausdorff, second-countable, boundaryless oriented and time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]]. Its smooth real $k$-forms are sections of $\bigwedge^kT^*M$, written $\Omega^k(M)$, and $d$ is the exterior derivative of [[lem-emg-lorentz-hodge-calculus]]. A smooth two-form $F$ is **closed** when $dF=0$ and **exact** when $F=dA$ for some smooth real one-form $A$ on the whole base.

By [[def-de-rham-cohomology]], $H^2_{\mathrm{dR}}(M)=Z^2(M)/B^2(M)$, where $Z^2(M)$ is the vector space of closed smooth two-forms and $B^2(M)$ is the vector space of exact smooth two-forms. Thus, for closed $F$, the statement $[F]=0$ means exactly that $F=dA$ for a global smooth one-form $A$. This equivalence is the quotient definition; it does not assert that every closed form is exact.

Identify $\mathbb C$ with $\mathbb R^2$ by $z=x+iy$ and set $U(1)=S^1:=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x^2+y^2=1\}$. Its topology is the subspace topology. Specify its smooth structure by the four charts

$$V_{x,\epsilon}=\{(x,y)\in S^1:\epsilon x>0\},\quad (x,y)\mapsto y,\quad y\mapsto(\epsilon\sqrt{1-y^2},y),$$

and

$$V_{y,\epsilon}=\{(x,y)\in S^1:\epsilon y>0\},\quad (x,y)\mapsto x,\quad x\mapsto(x,\epsilon\sqrt{1-x^2}),$$

for $\epsilon\in\{-1,1\}$, with each coordinate range $(-1,1)$. They cover $S^1$; their transition maps are restrictions of the positive square-root branch and coordinate projections, hence are smooth by [[lem-emg-positive-square-root-smoothness]] and [[thm-ck-euclidean-maps-closed-under-algebra-and-composition]]. In these coordinates multiplication is the restriction of $(x,y)(u,v)=(xu-yv,xv+yu)$ and inversion is $(x,y)\mapsto(x,-y)$, so both are smooth; they are also continuous for the stated topology. Thus this is a smooth Lie group and, in particular, a topological group as required by [[def-principal-g-bundle-and-associated-fiber-bundle]].

Let $E:\mathbb R\to U(1)$ be $E(t)=e^{it}=(\cos t,\sin t)$; the Cartesian formula is [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]. The trigonometric derivative identities of [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]], iterated, show that $E$ is smooth in the $C^\infty$ sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]: every derivative of either coordinate is $\pm\sin$ or $\pm\cos$, and these functions are continuous by [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]]. Surjectivity is [[thm-sine-and-cosine-parametrize-the-unit-circle]]. If $E(t)\in V_{x,\epsilon}$, the chart coordinate $\sin t$ has derivative $\cos t=x\ne0$; if $E(t)\in V_{y,\epsilon}$, the coordinate $\cos t$ has derivative $-\sin t=-y\ne0$. The smooth inverse-function theorem [[lem-choice-free-smooth-inverse-function-theorem-in-euclidean-space]] therefore makes $E$ a diffeomorphism from some open interval about $t$ onto an open circle arc. Every smooth map from an open subset of $M$ to $U(1)$ consequently has, near each point, a smooth real phase lift obtained by composing with such a local inverse.

A **normalized circle-connection datum** on $M$ consists of a supplied countable open cover $(U_i)_{i\in I}$, smooth transition maps $g_{ij}:U_i\cap U_j\to U(1)$, smooth real one-forms $a_i\in\Omega^1(U_i)$, and a fixed constant $\kappa_0>0$. Require $g_{ii}=1$ and $g_{ij}g_{jk}=g_{ik}$ on every triple intersection. Around each point of $U_i\cap U_j$, take any smooth real phase lift $f_{ij}$ with $g_{ij}=e^{if_{ij}}$; require

$$
a_j=a_i+df_{ij}
$$

on every such phase-lift neighborhood. If $f$ and $\widetilde f$ are two lifts on a connected neighborhood, [[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]] gives $f-\widetilde f\in2\pi\mathbb Z$ pointwise; continuity makes this difference constant, so $df=d\widetilde f$. Thus the compatibility condition is independent of the chosen lift. The globally defined form $\lambda(g):=-i\,g^{-1}dg$ is real, and [[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]] together with [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]] gives $\lambda(g)=df$ on every phase-lift neighborhood. Hence the equivalent lift-free condition is $a_j=a_i+\lambda(g_{ij})$.

The right principal $U(1)$-bundle convention is as defined in [[def-principal-g-bundle-and-associated-fiber-bundle]]: it has a continuous right action and locally trivial equivariant product charts, with free and transitive action on each fibre. The compatible transition functions are the gluing data for such a bundle, in the convention that a point with fibre coordinate $z_i$ in chart $i$ has coordinate $z_j=g_{ij}^{-1}z_i$ in chart $j$. No global real-valued angle on $U(1)$ is assumed.

The constant $\kappa_0$ is a chosen normalization with units of webers; it is not Planck's constant and is not a unit of electric charge. On a chart whose coordinates have length units, the normalized connection components $a_i$ have units $\mathrm m^{-1}$; the corresponding local potential $A_i:=\kappa_0a_i$ has components $\mathrm{Wb}\,\mathrm m^{-1}$, and its curvature $F_i:=dA_i=\kappa_0\,da_i$ has components $\mathrm{Wb}\,\mathrm m^{-2}$. This definition imposes no flux or charge quantization.

Let $G$ be a topological group, as in [[def-topological-group]], with identity $1$. A **right principal $G$-bundle** is a continuous map $\pi:P\to B$ with a continuous right action $(p,g)\mapsto pg$, satisfying $p1=p$, $(pg)h=p(gh)$ and $\pi(pg)=\pi(p)$, together with equivariant bundle charts $\theta_i:\pi^{-1}(U_i)\cong U_i\times G$ over an open cover. Equivariance means $\theta_i(pg)=(b,ag)$ whenever $\theta_i(p)=(b,a)$. Charts use ordinary products as in [[def-locally-trivial-fiber-bundle]]. In each fiber the action is free and transitive: right multiplication on $G$ has those properties and the chart identifies the actions. Freeness alone is not the definition.

A **left $G$-space** is a topological space $F$ with a continuous map $(g,x)\mapsto gx$ such that $1x=x$ and $g(hx)=(gh)x$. Effectiveness of this action is not required. Define
$$P\times_G F=(P\times F)/\bigl((pg,x)\sim(p,gx)\bigr)$$
with the ordinary quotient topology, and write $[p,x]$ for its points. Precisely, the relation is the orbit relation of the right action $(p,x)\cdot g=(pg,g^{-1}x)$. Its action law is $((p,x)\cdot g)\cdot h=(pgh,h^{-1}g^{-1}x)=(p,x)\cdot(gh)$, and its generating relations are exactly the displayed ones. Thus the equivalence relation and quotient are defined without choosing orbit representatives.

The projection $r([p,x])=\pi(p)$ is well-defined and continuous by [[thm-quotient-universal-property]], since $(p,x)\mapsto\pi(p)$ is continuous and constant on every orbit. This is the **associated fiber-bundle construction**; the next proposition proves its local triviality and pullback property. The quotient construction and projection already make sense before that proof.

If $B$ is empty then $P$ is empty. If $F$ is empty the associated space is empty even for nonempty $B$; this is allowed by our bundle convention. For singleton $F$ the construction is the orbit projection of the principal bundle. For the trivial group it is the product with $F$ over the chart-identified base. No AC is used.

Let $(M,g,N,o)$ have the oriented, time-oriented Lorentzian structure and volume form of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]]. On decomposable $k$-covectors define the induced exterior pairing by

$$\langle\alpha_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\alpha_k,\beta_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\beta_k\rangle_g:=\det\bigl(g^{-1}(\alpha_i,\beta_j)\bigr),$$

and extend it bilinearly. For $0\le k\le4$, its coordinate expression is the pointwise exterior metric on $k$-covectors

$$\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_g:=\frac1{k!}\alpha_{a_1\cdots a_k}\beta^{a_1\cdots a_k},$$

where indices are raised by $g^{-1}$. There is a unique smooth bundle map $\star_g:\Omega^k(M)\to\Omega^{4-k}(M)$ characterized by

$$\alpha\wedge\star_g\beta=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_g\,\mathrm{vol}_g$$

at every point. In a positively oriented $g$-orthonormal coframe $(e^0,e^1,e^2,e^3)$, put $\epsilon_0=-1$ and $\epsilon_1=\epsilon_2=\epsilon_3=1$. For an increasing index set $I\subseteq\{0,1,2,3\}$, let $I^c$ be its increasing complement, let $s(I,I^c)$ be the sign of the permutation $(I,I^c)$ to $(0,1,2,3)$, and set $\epsilon_I:=\prod_{i\in I}\epsilon_i$. Then

$$\star_g e^I=\epsilon_I s(I,I^c)e^{I^c}.$$

Consequently, on $k$-forms,

$$\star_g^2=(-1)^{k(4-k)+1}\operatorname{id}.$$

In particular $\star_g^2=-\operatorname{id}$ on two-forms. For a two-form $F$, the component formula in a positively oriented chart is

$$({\star_gF})_{ab}=\frac12(\mathrm{vol}_g)_{abcd}F^{cd}.$$

The exterior derivative in [[def-exterior-derivative-by-the-invariant-vector-field-formula]] has the local coordinate formula of [[thm-local-coordinate-formula-for-the-exterior-derivative]], satisfies $d^2=0$, and obeys the graded product rule of [[thm-the-exterior-derivative-is-a-graded-derivation]].

Use the first-order language of [[def-language-of-set-theory]]: all quantified objects are sets, and a **definable class** $\{x:\varphi(x,p)\}$ abbreviates a formula with set parameters $p$. It is not a new set or a domain for unrestricted quantification. Work with the usual set axioms, in particular [[def-axiom-of-power-set]] and [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]], and the ordered pairs, products and functions of [[def-ordered-pair]], [[def-cartesian-product]] and [[def-function]]. The power-set axiom supplies a collecting set; Separation trims it to exactly $\mathcal P(X)=\{Y:Y\subseteq X\}$.

A **small category** has a set $O$ of objects, a set $A$ of arrows, source and target functions $s,t:A\to O$, an identity function $e:O\to A$, and a composition function on the set $\{(a,b)\in A\times A:s(a)=t(b)\}$, where $ab$ denotes $a\circ b$ and the laws are $s(e(x))=t(e(x))=x$, $s(ab)=s(b)$, $t(ab)=t(a)$, $e(t(a))a=a=ae(s(a))$, and $(ab)c=a(bc)$ whenever the displayed compositions are defined. It is **locally small** when each specified hom-collection is a set. A definable large category is a schema of formulas for its objects, arrows and operations, with those laws asserted as formulas; it is not a set of all objects or a category of all large categories. No Grothendieck universe is assumed.

All indexed families in the local bundle construction have a supplied set index $I$. If $U_i\subseteq M$ and $G$ is a set, their tagged disjoint union is the subset $D=\{(i,x,z)\in I\times M\times G:x\in U_i\}$, formed by Separation. Given a set equivalence relation $E\subseteq D\times D$, each class $[u]_E=\{v\in D:(u,v)\in E\}$ is a subset of $D$, and the quotient is the set

$$
D/E=\{C\in\mathcal P(D):\exists u\in D\ \forall v\in D\ (v\in C\iff(u,v)\in E)\}.
$$

Thus the quotient is obtained by Separation in $\mathcal P(D)$, without choosing representatives. Transition-map graphs and connection data are subsets of specified finite products and power sets, not arbitrary proper-class objects.

For the Cauchy-development coding application, fix a set manifold $\Sigma$ and the tensor-bundle total spaces over $\Sigma\times\mathbb R$. A code consists of an open set $D\subseteq\Sigma\times\mathbb R$, graphs of a metric and a two-form on $D$ inside those fixed total spaces, a time orientation, and a fixed initial embedding. All of its coordinates belong to fixed products and power sets. Separation selects the tuples satisfying the specified smoothness, Lorentzian, field-equation and initial-data formulas. Hence these codes form a set. This size assertion does not prove field-equation existence, maximality or uniqueness, and makes no proper-class representative choice.

derivations.claim: Form the set-sized disjoint union $\coprod_i(U_i\times U(1))$ and identify $(x,z_i)$ with $(x,g_{ij}^{-1}(x)z_i)$ in chart $j$. Reflexivity follows from $g_{ii}=1$; the cocycle gives $g_{ji}=g_{ij}^{-1}$ and shows that transfer from $i$ to $j$ to $k$ equals direct transfer from $i$ to $k$. Hence these identifications define an equivalence relation and a well-defined projection $\pi:P\to M$.

For fixed $i$, the quotient map restricts to a bijection from $U_i\times U(1)$ onto $\pi^{-1}(U_i)$: every representative over $x\in U_i$ transfers uniquely to chart $i$, and a transition loop acts as the identity by the cocycle. On overlaps the chart changes are $(x,z_i)\mapsto(x,g_{ij}^{-1}(x)z_i)$, smooth diffeomorphisms with smooth inverse. The quotient map is open because the saturation of any open set is a union of its images under these overlap diffeomorphisms; therefore the bijections are homeomorphisms and form a smooth atlas.

Distinct base points have disjoint preimage neighborhoods because $M$ is Hausdorff. For two distinct points over the same base point, choose a chart containing that base point and disjoint fibre neighborhoods in $U(1)$; their products with a common base neighborhood separate the total-space points. Thus $P$ is Hausdorff. Fix one countable base $(B_n)$ of $M$ and the explicit countable base $(C_m)$ of circle arcs obtained by intersecting $U(1)\subset\mathbb R^2$ with rational open rectangles. In chart $i$, the products $(B_n\cap U_i)\times C_m$ form a base. Their images under the open charts form a base of $P$ indexed by the countable set $I\times\mathbb N\times\mathbb N$, which has an explicit finite-product enumeration. Thus $P$ is second countable, without selecting separate bases for a countable family of spaces.

Define the right action by $[x,z_i]\cdot\zeta=[x,z_i\zeta]$. It is well-defined because the chart transition is left multiplication by $g_{ij}^{-1}$ and hence commutes with right multiplication. In each chart it is smooth; it is free and transitive on every fibre. The charts in step 2.1 are equivariant, so $P\to M$ satisfies the principal-bundle definition in [F2].

Let $\eta=-i z^{-1}dz$ be the real invariant one-form on $U(1)$, normalized by $\eta(\partial_\theta)=1$ for the local angle $z=e^{i\theta}$. In chart $i$ set $\omega_i=\eta+a_i$. If $z_j=g_{ij}^{-1}z_i$, then $\eta_j=\eta_i-\lambda(g_{ij})$, while [F1] gives $a_j=a_i+\lambda(g_{ij})$; thus $\omega_j=\omega_i$ on every overlap and the local forms define a global smooth one-form $\omega$. Its value on the vertical generator is $1$, it is right invariant, and in every chart $\ker\omega_i$ is a complement to the vertical line, since for each base tangent vector there is a unique circle tangent vector cancelling $a_i$. Hence $\omega$ is a principal connection.

In chart $i$, $d\omega=d a_i$ because $d\eta=0$. On overlaps $d a_j=d a_i+d\lambda(g_{ij})=d a_i$, since locally $\lambda(g_{ij})=df_{ij}$ and $d^2f_{ij}=0$ by [F3]. The forms $da_i$ therefore glue to a global two-form $f$, and the local identity $d\omega=\pi^*f$ proves the curvature is basic and closed. Multiplication by the fixed constant $\kappa_0$ gives $A_i=\kappa_0a_i$ and $F=\kappa_0f$ with $dA_i=F$.

If $(a_i')$ is another compatible family for the same transition maps, then $(a_j'-a_j)-(a_i'-a_i)=0$ on each overlap. Thus the differences patch to a global one-form $\alpha$ on $M$. Conversely, adding any global one-form $\alpha$ to every $a_i$ preserves $a_j=a_i+\lambda(g_{ij})$ and changes curvature from $f$ to $f+d\alpha$ without changing the transition data. This proves the fixed-bundle variation claim.

boundaries.evidence: Statement permits a smooth empty base. Proof step 1.1 then forms the empty tagged union and quotient, and the chart/curvature assertions in steps 2.1 and 4.1 have no base point or local form to test.

Proof steps 3.3 and 4.1 give omega_i=eta+a_i and f|Ui=da_i. For zero compatible a_i, their derivatives and the physical curvature kappa0*f vanish; transitions must still satisfy the stated compatibility.
Proof steps 1.1 and 2.1 for a one-set cover have only g_ii=1, so P is its single product chart U_i times U(1). Step 3.3 defines eta+a_i on that chart, including its permitted nonzero a_i.

Proof steps 1.1 and 2.1 use the cocycle only where an overlap exists; empty overlaps impose no relation. Constant or disconnected-overlap transitions still have smooth inverse chart changes, so connectedness is not assumed.

boundaries.reason: The Statement is a bundle-gluing result over a smooth manifold with countable open cover, not an interval evolution or path-transport theorem. No distinguished parameter endpoint is present.

boundaries.evidence: Proof step 1.1 uses actual equivalence classes, step 2.1 uses unique transport into a fixed chart, and step 3.1 uses one fixed base of M with explicit rational-circle rectangles. No representatives or separate countable family of chart bases is chosen.
Proof step 5.1 subtracts the two same-transition compatibility equations; all overlap differences agree, hence patch to one global base one-form. This is the forward fixed-sector variation direction.

Proof step 5.1 adds a supplied global base one-form alpha to every a_i; its restrictions cancel on overlaps, preserving the original transition rule and changing curvature from f to f+dalpha. This is the reverse fixed-sector variation direction.

Use the real ordered field of [[def-real-numbers]] and [[def-complete-ordered-field]]. For a nonempty set $S\subseteq\mathbb R$ bounded above, $\sup S$ denotes the unique real upper bound $u$ such that $u\le v$ for every upper bound $v$. Existence is the least-upper-bound property established for these reals by [[thm-reals-cauchy-complete]]; if $u,u'$ both satisfy it, $u\le u'$ and $u'\le u$ imply equality. The notation is restricted to this domain.

For nonempty $S$ bounded below, use [[def-infimum]] and [[thm-infimum-property]]: $\inf S=-\sup(-S)$, where $-S=\{-s:s\in S\}$. Indeed a lower bound $l$ for $S$ gives the upper bound $-l$ for $-S$; negating its least upper bound gives a lower bound for $S$ greater than every other one.

Neither $\sup\varnothing$ nor $\inf\varnothing$ is defined in $\mathbb R$: every real is an upper and lower bound, with no least upper or greatest lower bound. If another construction stipulates the value zero for an empty path family, that stipulation is a separate total definition, not $\sup\varnothing=0$. Infinite values require an explicitly specified extended ordered set; no extended-real field operations are introduced here.

Let $X$ be a set and use the ordered real field of [[def-real-numbers]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]] and [[def-ordered-field]]. In the convention of [[def-metric-space]], a **real metric** is a function $d:X\times X\to\mathbb R$ satisfying, for all $x,y,z\in X$, separation $d(x,y)=0\iff x=y$, symmetry $d(x,y)=d(y,x)$ and the triangle inequality $d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)$. A **real pseudometric** replaces separation by $d(x,x)=0$ and retains the other two axioms. All values are finite real numbers. Neither definition assumes nonnegativity as an additional axiom.

For either structure, put $B_d(x,r)=\{y\in X:d(x,y)<r\}$ for real $r>0$. The induced topology consists of the subsets $O\subseteq X$ for which every $x\in O$ admits $r>0$ with $B_d(x,r)\subseteq O$. After the nonnegativity deduction in the well-definedness lemma, these balls form a basis: $x\in B_d(x,r)$ by reflexivity, and if $z\in B_d(x,r)\cap B_d(y,s)$, the positive radius $t=\min\{r-d(x,z),s-d(y,z)\}$ has $B_d(z,t)$ contained in that intersection by the triangle inequality. This argument also works for pseudometrics and for empty $X$ (the empty topology). No infinite-distance, semimetric or quasimetric convention is consumed.

Let $M$ be a smooth Hausdorff second-countable manifold **without boundary**, in the sense of [[def-smooth-manifold]]. Let $g$ be a positive definite smooth Riemannian metric as in [[def-riemannian-metric-symmetric-cotangent-connection-and-covariant-hessian]]. Use the Levi-Civita connection of [[def-levi-civita-connection]] with the existence and coordinate formula supplied by [[prop-christoffel-formula-for-the-levi-civita-connection]]; in coordinates it has coefficients $\Gamma^k_{ij}=\frac12g^{kl}(\partial_i g_{jl}+\partial_j g_{il}-\partial_l g_{ij})$. A parametrized affine geodesic is a smooth curve $\gamma:J\to M$ on an interval with nonempty interior satisfying $\nabla_{\dot\gamma}\dot\gamma=0$, equivalently $\ddot\gamma^k+\Gamma^k_{ij}(\gamma)\dot\gamma^i\dot\gamma^j=0$, where covariant differentiation along the curve is defined by [[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]; the coordinate equation is the expansion of that derivative in a coordinate basis. Its maximal domain is an interval on which it cannot be extended with the same affine parameter as a solution. **Two-sided geodesic completeness** means that every maximal affine geodesic is defined on all of $\mathbb R$.

Independently, for a real metric $d$ in [[def-metric-space]], a sequence $(x_n)$ is Cauchy when for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $N$ with $d(x_m,x_n)<\varepsilon$ whenever $m,n\ge N$. It converges to $x$ when for every $\varepsilon>0$ eventually $d(x_n,x)<\varepsilon$. **Metric completeness** means that every Cauchy sequence converges in the given metric space. In a Riemannian application the metric must be the distance induced by $g$ on a connected component: the infimum of lengths $\int\sqrt{g(\dot\alpha,\dot\alpha)}\,dt$ over piecewise-$C^1$ connecting curves. Its definition and finite metric property are supplied by [[def-riemannian-distance-on-a-connected-manifold]] and [[thm-riemannian-distance-is-a-metric]]. Specify that induced metric, rather than an arbitrary compatible metric. Distinct components are treated separately; no infinite distance is inserted into a real metric.

These are different completeness conditions. Their equivalence is a Hopf–Rinow theorem requiring its own hypotheses and proof; it is not part of this definition. In particular, a Lorentzian metric is not a positive definite distance, and this convention supplies no Lorentzian Hopf–Rinow implication.

The boundaryless restriction matters: the Euclidean interval $[0,1]$ is metrically complete, while the curve $\gamma(t)=1/2+t$ stays inside it only for $-1/2\le t\le1/2$ and cannot be continued there as a two-sided affine geodesic with velocity $1$. Completeness of this interval follows because a real Cauchy sequence converges in $\mathbb R$ by [[thm-reals-cauchy-complete]] and its limit remains between $0$ and $1$. This boundary example explains the domain restriction; it is not an instance of the boundaryless equivalence.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold, possibly with boundary. For $k\ge1$, $c\in C_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$ and $\omega\in\Omega^{k-1}(M)$, define integration over a chain by the finite linear sum of its simplex integrals. Then
$$\int_c d\omega=\int_{\partial c}\omega.$$
The zero chain has integral zero. In degree zero the boundary is zero; no degree-minus-one form is required by this statement.

Let $(M,g,N,o)$ be the smooth, Hausdorff, second-countable, boundaryless oriented and time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]]. Its smooth real $k$-forms are sections of $\bigwedge^kT^*M$, written $\Omega^k(M)$, and $d$ is the exterior derivative of [[lem-emg-lorentz-hodge-calculus]]. A smooth two-form $F$ is **closed** when $dF=0$ and **exact** when $F=dA$ for some smooth real one-form $A$ on the whole base.

By [[def-de-rham-cohomology]], $H^2_{\mathrm{dR}}(M)=Z^2(M)/B^2(M)$, where $Z^2(M)$ is the vector space of closed smooth two-forms and $B^2(M)$ is the vector space of exact smooth two-forms. Thus, for closed $F$, the statement $[F]=0$ means exactly that $F=dA$ for a global smooth one-form $A$. This equivalence is the quotient definition; it does not assert that every closed form is exact.

Identify $\mathbb C$ with $\mathbb R^2$ by $z=x+iy$ and set $U(1)=S^1:=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x^2+y^2=1\}$. Its topology is the subspace topology. Specify its smooth structure by the four charts

$$V_{x,\epsilon}=\{(x,y)\in S^1:\epsilon x>0\},\quad (x,y)\mapsto y,\quad y\mapsto(\epsilon\sqrt{1-y^2},y),$$

and

$$V_{y,\epsilon}=\{(x,y)\in S^1:\epsilon y>0\},\quad (x,y)\mapsto x,\quad x\mapsto(x,\epsilon\sqrt{1-x^2}),$$

for $\epsilon\in\{-1,1\}$, with each coordinate range $(-1,1)$. They cover $S^1$; their transition maps are restrictions of the positive square-root branch and coordinate projections, hence are smooth by [[lem-emg-positive-square-root-smoothness]] and [[thm-ck-euclidean-maps-closed-under-algebra-and-composition]]. In these coordinates multiplication is the restriction of $(x,y)(u,v)=(xu-yv,xv+yu)$ and inversion is $(x,y)\mapsto(x,-y)$, so both are smooth; they are also continuous for the stated topology. Thus this is a smooth Lie group and, in particular, a topological group as required by [[def-principal-g-bundle-and-associated-fiber-bundle]].

Let $E:\mathbb R\to U(1)$ be $E(t)=e^{it}=(\cos t,\sin t)$; the Cartesian formula is [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]. The trigonometric derivative identities of [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]], iterated, show that $E$ is smooth in the $C^\infty$ sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]: every derivative of either coordinate is $\pm\sin$ or $\pm\cos$, and these functions are continuous by [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]]. Surjectivity is [[thm-sine-and-cosine-parametrize-the-unit-circle]]. If $E(t)\in V_{x,\epsilon}$, the chart coordinate $\sin t$ has derivative $\cos t=x\ne0$; if $E(t)\in V_{y,\epsilon}$, the coordinate $\cos t$ has derivative $-\sin t=-y\ne0$. The smooth inverse-function theorem [[lem-choice-free-smooth-inverse-function-theorem-in-euclidean-space]] therefore makes $E$ a diffeomorphism from some open interval about $t$ onto an open circle arc. Every smooth map from an open subset of $M$ to $U(1)$ consequently has, near each point, a smooth real phase lift obtained by composing with such a local inverse.

A **normalized circle-connection datum** on $M$ consists of a supplied countable open cover $(U_i)_{i\in I}$, smooth transition maps $g_{ij}:U_i\cap U_j\to U(1)$, smooth real one-forms $a_i\in\Omega^1(U_i)$, and a fixed constant $\kappa_0>0$. Require $g_{ii}=1$ and $g_{ij}g_{jk}=g_{ik}$ on every triple intersection. Around each point of $U_i\cap U_j$, take any smooth real phase lift $f_{ij}$ with $g_{ij}=e^{if_{ij}}$; require

$$
a_j=a_i+df_{ij}
$$

on every such phase-lift neighborhood. If $f$ and $\widetilde f$ are two lifts on a connected neighborhood, [[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]] gives $f-\widetilde f\in2\pi\mathbb Z$ pointwise; continuity makes this difference constant, so $df=d\widetilde f$. Thus the compatibility condition is independent of the chosen lift. The globally defined form $\lambda(g):=-i\,g^{-1}dg$ is real, and [[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]] together with [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]] gives $\lambda(g)=df$ on every phase-lift neighborhood. Hence the equivalent lift-free condition is $a_j=a_i+\lambda(g_{ij})$.

The right principal $U(1)$-bundle convention is as defined in [[def-principal-g-bundle-and-associated-fiber-bundle]]: it has a continuous right action and locally trivial equivariant product charts, with free and transitive action on each fibre. The compatible transition functions are the gluing data for such a bundle, in the convention that a point with fibre coordinate $z_i$ in chart $i$ has coordinate $z_j=g_{ij}^{-1}z_i$ in chart $j$. No global real-valued angle on $U(1)$ is assumed.

The constant $\kappa_0$ is a chosen normalization with units of webers; it is not Planck's constant and is not a unit of electric charge. On a chart whose coordinates have length units, the normalized connection components $a_i$ have units $\mathrm m^{-1}$; the corresponding local potential $A_i:=\kappa_0a_i$ has components $\mathrm{Wb}\,\mathrm m^{-1}$, and its curvature $F_i:=dA_i=\kappa_0\,da_i$ has components $\mathrm{Wb}\,\mathrm m^{-2}$. This definition imposes no flux or charge quantization.

Let $(M,g,N,o)$ have the oriented, time-oriented Lorentzian structure and volume form of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]]. On decomposable $k$-covectors define the induced exterior pairing by

$$\langle\alpha_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\alpha_k,\beta_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\beta_k\rangle_g:=\det\bigl(g^{-1}(\alpha_i,\beta_j)\bigr),$$

and extend it bilinearly. For $0\le k\le4$, its coordinate expression is the pointwise exterior metric on $k$-covectors

$$\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_g:=\frac1{k!}\alpha_{a_1\cdots a_k}\beta^{a_1\cdots a_k},$$

where indices are raised by $g^{-1}$. There is a unique smooth bundle map $\star_g:\Omega^k(M)\to\Omega^{4-k}(M)$ characterized by

$$\alpha\wedge\star_g\beta=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_g\,\mathrm{vol}_g$$

at every point. In a positively oriented $g$-orthonormal coframe $(e^0,e^1,e^2,e^3)$, put $\epsilon_0=-1$ and $\epsilon_1=\epsilon_2=\epsilon_3=1$. For an increasing index set $I\subseteq\{0,1,2,3\}$, let $I^c$ be its increasing complement, let $s(I,I^c)$ be the sign of the permutation $(I,I^c)$ to $(0,1,2,3)$, and set $\epsilon_I:=\prod_{i\in I}\epsilon_i$. Then

$$\star_g e^I=\epsilon_I s(I,I^c)e^{I^c}.$$

Consequently, on $k$-forms,

$$\star_g^2=(-1)^{k(4-k)+1}\operatorname{id}.$$

In particular $\star_g^2=-\operatorname{id}$ on two-forms. For a two-form $F$, the component formula in a positively oriented chart is

$$({\star_gF})_{ab}=\frac12(\mathrm{vol}_g)_{abcd}F^{cd}.$$

The exterior derivative in [[def-exterior-derivative-by-the-invariant-vector-field-formula]] has the local coordinate formula of [[thm-local-coordinate-formula-for-the-exterior-derivative]], satisfies $d^2=0$, and obeys the graded product rule of [[thm-the-exterior-derivative-is-a-graded-derivation]].

Let $\mathbb{R}$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).
For every $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \ge 0$ and every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with
$n \ge 1$ there is a **unique** $s \in \mathbb{R}$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^n = a$
([[def-integer-power]]); we write

$$s = a^{1/n} = \sqrt[n]{a}.$$

Moreover $a^{1/n} > 0$ when $a > 0$, and $a^{1/1} = a$.

**This generalises the published [[thm-of-square-roots]], and the case $n = 2$ is
not new.** That theorem already produces the unique $\sqrt{a} \ge 0$ with
$(\sqrt{a})^2 = a$, and it is cited as such throughout the library; the notation
$a^{1/2}$ introduced here is the same number. What is new is the passage to
general $n$: the completed square that drives the $n = 2$ argument has no direct
analogue, and its place is taken by the factorisation of $b^n - a^n$ and the
resulting Lipschitz estimate ([[lem-power-difference-factorisation]]).

In ZF, let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be smooth, and let $a\in U$. If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open neighbourhoods $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that $f|_V:V\to W$ is a diffeomorphism. Writing $g=(f|_V)^{-1}$,
$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$
No choice axiom is used.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]), let $F$ be its integral function
([[def-the-integral-function]]), and let $c \in [a,b]$ be a point at which $f$ is
continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $F$ is differentiable at $c$ as a
function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$F'(c) \;=\; f(c) .$$

At $c = a$ and $c = b$ this is the one-sided statement, which is what
[[def-derivative]] means at those points: every point of a nondegenerate interval
is a limit point of it, so $F'(c)$ is a meaningful symbol at every $c \in [a,b]$,
and the difference quotient is taken over $[a,b] \setminus \{c\}$.

**Consequently, if $f$ is continuous on the whole of $[a,b]$, then $F$ is a
primitive of $f$ there**: $F' = f$ at every point of $[a,b]$.

**Continuity at $c$ is a hypothesis and it cannot be dropped.** For an integrable
$f$ that is discontinuous at $c$, $F'(c)$ may fail to exist, and it may exist and
differ from $f(c)$; both are exhibited on the companion page, by
an integrable function with no primitive and by a false
statement about the integral function.

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

$$

$$

Let $U_N=\{(x^0,x,y,z)\in M:r+z>0\}$ and $U_S=\{(x^0,x,y,z)\in M:r-z>0\}$; these two open sets cover $M$. Then $dF_b=0$ and its flux through the unit sphere with outward orientation is $4\pi b$. If $b\ne0$, $F_b$ has no global one-form potential on $M$. On $U_N$ and $U_S$,

$$
A_N=b(1-\cos\theta)\,d\phi,\qquad A_S=-b(1+\cos\theta)\,d\phi
$$

are smooth local potentials with $dA_N=dA_S=F_b$, and $A_S-A_N=-2b\,d\phi$ on the overlap. For a chosen normalization $\kappa_0>0$, these local forms define the normalized circle-connection data of [[def-emg-local-potentials-and-circle-data]] precisely when the transition $g_{NS}=e^{-2ib\phi/\kappa_0}$ is single-valued, equivalently $2b/\kappa_0\in\mathbb Z$. For a smooth loop $g(e^{i\phi})=e^{i\chi(\phi)}$, its winding is $[\chi(2\pi)-\chi(0)]/(2\pi)$, with both circles oriented by increasing angle. The transition winding has sign $-2b/\kappa_0$ in the stated north-to-south convention, while $\int_{S^2}F_b/(2\pi\kappa_0)=2b/\kappa_0$. This is an exact condition for this chosen circle normalization, not a claim that every classical real flux is quantized. For a nonempty set $S\subseteq\mathbb R$ bounded above, $\sup S$ denotes the unique real upper bound $u$ such that $u\le v$ for every upper bound $v$. Existence is the least-upper-bound property established for these reals by [[thm-reals-cauchy-complete]]; if $u,u'$ both satisfy it, $u\le u'$ and $u'\le u$ imply equality. The notation is restricted to this domain.

For nonempty $S$ bounded below, use [[def-infimum]] and [[thm-infimum-property]]: $\inf S=-\sup(-S)$, where $-S=\{-s:s\in S\}$. Indeed a lower bound $l$ for $S$ gives the upper bound $-l$ for $-S$; negating its least upper bound gives a lower bound for $S$ greater than every other one.

Neither $\sup\varnothing$ nor $\inf\varnothing$ is defined in $\mathbb R$: every real is an upper and lower bound, with no least upper or greatest lower bound. If another construction stipulates the value zero for an empty path family, that stipulation is a separate total definition, not $\sup\varnothing=0$. Infinite values require an explicitly specified extended ordered set; no extended-real field operations are introduced here.

Let $M$ be a smooth Hausdorff second-countable manifold **without boundary**, in the sense of [[def-smooth-manifold]]. Let $g$ be a positive definite smooth Riemannian metric as in [[def-riemannian-metric-symmetric-cotangent-connection-and-covariant-hessian]]. Use the Levi-Civita connection of [[def-levi-civita-connection]] with the existence and coordinate formula supplied by [[prop-christoffel-formula-for-the-levi-civita-connection]]; in coordinates it has coefficients $\Gamma^k_{ij}=\frac12g^{kl}(\partial_i g_{jl}+\partial_j g_{il}-\partial_l g_{ij})$. A parametrized affine geodesic is a smooth curve $\gamma:J\to M$ on an interval with nonempty interior satisfying $\nabla_{\dot\gamma}\dot\gamma=0$, equivalently $\ddot\gamma^k+\Gamma^k_{ij}(\gamma)\dot\gamma^i\dot\gamma^j=0$, where covariant differentiation along the curve is defined by [[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]; the coordinate equation is the expansion of that derivative in a coordinate basis. Its maximal domain is an interval on which it cannot be extended with the same affine parameter as a solution. **Two-sided geodesic completeness** means that every maximal affine geodesic is defined on all of $\mathbb R$.

Independently, for a real metric $d$ in [[def-metric-space]], a sequence $(x_n)$ is Cauchy when for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $N$ with $d(x_m,x_n)<\varepsilon$ whenever $m,n\ge N$. It converges to $x$ when for every $\varepsilon>0$ eventually $d(x_n,x)<\varepsilon$. **Metric completeness** means that every Cauchy sequence converges in the given metric space. In a Riemannian application the metric must be the distance induced by $g$ on a connected component: the infimum of lengths $\int\sqrt{g(\dot\alpha,\dot\alpha)}\,dt$ over piecewise-$C^1$ connecting curves. Its definition and finite metric property are supplied by [[def-riemannian-distance-on-a-connected-manifold]] and [[thm-riemannian-distance-is-a-metric]]. Specify that induced metric, rather than an arbitrary compatible metric. Distinct components are treated separately; no infinite distance is inserted into a real metric.

These are different completeness conditions. Their equivalence is a Hopf–Rinow theorem requiring its own hypotheses and proof; it is not part of this definition. In particular, a Lorentzian metric is not a positive definite distance, and this convention supplies no Lorentzian Hopf–Rinow implication.

The boundaryless restriction matters: the Euclidean interval $[0,1]$ is metrically complete, while the curve $\gamma(t)=1/2+t$ stays inside it only for $-1/2\le t\le1/2$ and cannot be continued there as a two-sided affine geodesic with velocity $1$. Completeness of this interval follows because a real Cauchy sequence converges in $\mathbb R$ by [[thm-reals-cauchy-complete]] and its limit remains between $0$ and $1$. This boundary example explains the domain restriction; it is not an instance of the boundaryless equivalence.

In ZF, let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be smooth, and let $a\in U$. If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open neighbourhoods $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that $f|_V:V\to W$ is a diffeomorphism. Writing $g=(f|_V)^{-1}$,

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) with its order and absolute value
([[def-real-order]]).

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in \mathbb{R}$
be a **limit point** of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]), and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
We say that **$f(x)$ tends to $L$ as $x$ tends to $c$**, and write

$$\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L ,$$

when

$$(\forall \varepsilon > 0)\ (\exists \delta > 0)\ (\forall x \in A)\ \bigl[\ 0 < |x - c| < \delta \ \Longrightarrow\ |f(x) - L| < \varepsilon\ \bigr],$$

where $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$ range over the **positive reals**.

In the language of neighbourhoods ([[def-neighbourhood-r]]) the condition reads:
for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real $\delta > 0$ with

$$f\bigl(A \cap N^{*}_{\delta}(c)\bigr) \;\subseteq\; N_{\varepsilon}(L),$$

$N^{*}_{\delta}(c) = \{\, y : 0 < |y - c| < \delta \,\}$ being the punctured
$\delta$-neighbourhood of $c$ and $N_{\varepsilon}(L) = (L - \varepsilon,\ L +
\varepsilon)$ the open interval of [[def-interval]]. The two forms agree because
$|f(x) - L| < \varepsilon$ says exactly $f(x) \in N_\varepsilon(L)$, and
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ says exactly $x \in N^{*}_\delta(c)$.

**Three features of this definition are load bearing, not decoration.**

1. **$c$ is required to be a limit point of $A$.** By [[def-limit-point-r]] that
   says every punctured neighbourhood of $c$ meets $A$, so for every $\delta > 0$
   the set $A \cap N^{*}_\delta(c)$ over which the implication quantifies is
   nonempty. Drop the requirement and the implication can be satisfied
   vacuously by *every* real $L$ at once, which is exactly what
   [[fs-limit-unique-at-every-point-of-the-domain]] records. At a point of $A$
   that is not a limit point of $A$ — an isolated point — the symbol
   $\lim_{x \to c} f(x)$ is therefore **not defined** in this library.

2. **$c \in A$ is not required.** A limit point of $A$ need not belong to $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]), and the definition never evaluates $f$ at $c$. This
   is what allows a limit to be taken at a point where the function is not
   defined at all, as at $0$ for $x \mapsto x\,\psi(1/x)$.

3. **The value $f(c)$, when it exists, is irrelevant.** The hypothesis
   $0 < |x - c|$ excludes $x = c$ from the quantifier, so changing $f$ at the
   single point $c$ changes nothing. Equality of the limit with the value is an
   extra condition, not a consequence: [[fs-limit-equals-value]].

**The notation presumes uniqueness.** Writing $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L$ treats
the left-hand side as a name for a single real number, which is legitimate only
because at a limit point at most one $L$ can satisfy the displayed condition.
That obligation is discharged by [[lem-function-limit-unique]], recorded in this
item's `justified_by`. As with $\sup S$ ([[rem-sup-conventions]]) and
$\lim_k x_k$ ([[lem-limit-unique]]), the symbol is written only for a function
already known to have a limit at $c$.

**Real and rational $\varepsilon$ define the same relation.** Above,
$\varepsilon$ and $\delta$ range over the positive reals. Restricting either
quantifier to the positive rationals gives the same relation: every positive
rational is a positive real, and below every positive real lies a positive
rational ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]), so an $\varepsilon$-condition verified for
all positive rationals is verified for an arbitrary positive real $\eta$ by
running it at a rational $\varepsilon$ with $0 < \varepsilon < \eta$, and a
$\delta$ produced as a real may be shrunk to a rational one below it. This is
the passage sanctioned in the remarks of [[def-sequence]], and it is what lets
this definition be compared with [[def-real-limit]], whose $\varepsilon$ is
rational, in [[thm-sequential-criterion-for-function-limits]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}$, with neighbourhoods as in
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and closure as in
[[def-interior-closure-boundary-r]].

- $x$ is an **adherent point** of $A$ when $N_\varepsilon(x) \cap A \ne
  \varnothing$ for every real $\varepsilon > 0$.
- $x$ is a **limit point** (or *accumulation point*) of $A$ when
  $N^{*}_\varepsilon(x) \cap A \ne \varnothing$ for every real
  $\varepsilon > 0$: every punctured neighbourhood of $x$ meets $A$.
- $x$ is an **isolated point** of $A$ when $x \in A$ and there is a real
  $\varepsilon > 0$ with $N_\varepsilon(x) \cap A = \{x\}$.
- The **derived set** of $A$ is
  $$A' \;:=\; \{\, x \in \mathbb{R} : x \text{ is a limit point of } A \,\}.$$
- $A$ is **dense in $\mathbb{R}$** when $\overline{A} = \mathbb{R}$.

**A limit point is an adherent point**, since $N^{*}_\varepsilon(x) \subseteq
N_\varepsilon(x)$; and an element of $A$ is an adherent point of $A$, since
$x \in N_\varepsilon(x) \cap A$ ([[def-neighbourhood-r]]). So the adherent
points of $A$ are exactly the points of $A \cup A'$, a statement proved as part
of [[thm-closure-characterisations-r]].

**Limit point and isolated point are exact opposites inside $A$.** For
$x \in A$: $x$ is an isolated point of $A$ exactly when it is not a limit point
of $A$. Indeed $N_\varepsilon(x) \cap A = \{x\}$ says precisely that
$N^{*}_\varepsilon(x) \cap A = \varnothing$, because $x$ itself always lies in
$N_\varepsilon(x) \cap A$ when $x \in A$; so the existence of an $\varepsilon$
witnessing isolation is the negation of the condition defining a limit point.
A point of $A$ is therefore either isolated in $A$ or a limit point of $A$, and
never both.

**A limit point need not belong to the set, and a point of the set need not be a
limit point.** Both possibilities occur, and the two examples that matter later
are $0$, which is a limit point of $\{\, 1/k : k \ge 1 \,\}$ without belonging
to it, and $0$ again, which belongs to $\{0\} \cup [1,2]$ as an isolated point.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]) and its absolute value ([[def-abs-value]]).

Let $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $\varepsilon \in \mathbb{R}$ with
$\varepsilon > 0$. The **$\varepsilon$-neighbourhood of $x$** is

$$N_\varepsilon(x) \;:=\; \{\, y \in \mathbb{R} : |y - x| < \varepsilon \,\},$$

and the **punctured $\varepsilon$-neighbourhood of $x$** is

$$N^{*}_\varepsilon(x) \;:=\; N_\varepsilon(x) \setminus \{x\} \;=\; \{\, y \in \mathbb{R} : 0 < |y - x| < \varepsilon \,\}.$$

The two descriptions of $N^{*}_\varepsilon(x)$ agree because $|y - x| = 0$ holds
exactly when $y = x$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]]).

**A neighbourhood is an open interval.** For every $x$ and every
$\varepsilon > 0$,

$$N_\varepsilon(x) \;=\; (x - \varepsilon,\ x + \varepsilon),$$

the interval of [[def-interval]]. Indeed [[lem-of-abs-value]] gives, for
$\varepsilon > 0$, the equivalence $|y - x| < \varepsilon \iff -\varepsilon <
y - x < \varepsilon$, and adding $x$ throughout turns the right-hand side into
$x - \varepsilon < y < x + \varepsilon$ ([[def-ordered-field]]).

**The centre lies in its own neighbourhoods.** $x \in N_\varepsilon(x)$, since
$|x - x| = |0| = 0 < \varepsilon$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]]).

**Punctured neighbourhoods are never empty.** The element
$y := x + \varepsilon/2$ satisfies $|y - x| = \varepsilon/2$, which is
$> 0$ and $< \varepsilon$, so $y \in N^{*}_\varepsilon(x)$
([[lem-of-abs-value]], [[def-ordered-field]]).

**Monotonicity in the radius.** If $0 < \delta \le \varepsilon$ then
$N_\delta(x) \subseteq N_\varepsilon(x)$, because $|y - x| < \delta \le
\varepsilon$ ([[def-ordered-field]]).

**Nesting at an interior point.** If $y \in N_\varepsilon(x)$ and
$0 < \delta \le \varepsilon - |y - x|$, then

$$N_\delta(y) \;\subseteq\; N_\varepsilon(x).$$

Indeed for $z \in N_\delta(y)$ the triangle inequality
([[lem-of-triangle-inequality]]) gives
$|z - x| = |(z - y) + (y - x)| \le |z - y| + |y - x| < \delta + |y - x| \le
\varepsilon$. Note that $\varepsilon - |y - x| > 0$ precisely because
$y \in N_\varepsilon(x)$, so such a $\delta$ always exists.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]],
[[def-real-numbers]]) with its order and absolute value ([[def-real-order]]), and
$\mathbb{N}$ is the set of natural numbers with its order ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[def-nat-order]]).

A **sequence of reals** is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$. We write
$x_k$ for the value $x(k)$, call it the **$k$-th term**, and write $(x_k)$, or
$(x_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$, for the function itself. The **range** of $(x_k)$ is
the subset $\{\, x_k : k \in \mathbb{N} \,\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}$.

Let $(x_k)$ be a sequence of reals and let $P$ be a property of indices.

- $(x_k)$ is **bounded** if there is $M \in \mathbb{R}$ with $|x_k| \le M$ for
  every $k \in \mathbb{N}$; it is **unbounded** otherwise.
- $P$ holds **eventually** if there is $K \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $P(k)$ holds
  for every $k \ge K$.
- $P$ holds **frequently** if for every $K \in \mathbb{N}$ there is some
  $k \ge K$ for which $P(k)$ holds.
- For $K \in \mathbb{N}$, the **$K$-th tail** of $(x_k)$ is the sequence
  $x^{(K)}$ defined by $x^{(K)}_j := x_{j + K}$ for $j \in \mathbb{N}$; it is
  again a sequence of reals.
- A function $n : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ is **strictly increasing** if
  $n_j < n_k$ whenever $j < k$. For such an $n$, the **subsequence** of $(x_k)$
  along $n$ is the composite $x \circ n$, written $(x_{n_k})_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$;
  it is again a sequence of reals.

**Convergence and Cauchyness are not defined here.** They are already fixed, for
sequences of reals, by the published [[def-real-limit]]: $(x_k)$ *converges* to
$x \in \mathbb{R}$ when for every rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is
$K \in \mathbb{N}$ with $|x_k - x| < \varepsilon$ for all $k \ge K$, and $(x_k)$
is *Cauchy* when for every rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $K \in \mathbb{N}$
with $|x_k - x_l| < \varepsilon$ for all $k, l \ge K$. This page builds the
toolkit for those two notions and does not restate them. A sequence
**converges** if it converges to some real, and **diverges** if it does not.

A sequence $(x_k)$ of reals **converges** to $x \in \mathbb{R}$ when for
every rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $K$ with
$|x_k - x| < \hat\varepsilon$ for all $k \ge K$. It is **Cauchy** when for
every rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $K$ with
$|x_k - x_l| < \hat\varepsilon$ for all $k, l \ge K$.

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[def-real-numbers]]) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) and let
$\varepsilon \in F$ with $\varepsilon > 0$. Then there is a natural number
$n \ge 1$ such that

$$\frac{1}{n \cdot 1_F} < \varepsilon ,$$

where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of $F$ ([[thm-of-archimedean]]) and
$1/(n \cdot 1_F)$ is its multiplicative inverse ([[def-field]]). As is standard
we abbreviate $n \cdot 1_F$ to $n$ and write the conclusion $1/n < \varepsilon$.

This is the **reciprocal form** of the Archimedean property.
[[thm-of-archimedean]] on its own delivers only the assertion that the canonical
naturals are cofinal, $x < n \cdot 1_F$; the form actually used in analysis, that
the reciprocals of the naturals get below every positive bound, is the statement
above, and it is recorded separately so that no proof has to reconstruct the
inversion step in passing.

Every complete ordered field $F$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) is Archimedean:
for every $x \in F$ there is a natural number $n \ge 1$ with $x < n \cdot 1_F$,
where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of the ordered field $F$
([[def-ordered-field]]). Equivalently, the canonical naturals are cofinal in $F$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) with positive cone $P$, and
let $a, b \in F$.

1. If $a > 0$ then $a^{-1} > 0$.
2. If $0 < a < b$ then $0 < b^{-1} < a^{-1}$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field, with field structure as in [[def-field]], and for
$n \ge 1$ let $n \cdot 1_F$ denote the canonical natural number
$\underbrace{1_F + \cdots + 1_F}_{n}$, defined recursively by $1 \cdot 1_F = 1_F$
and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F = n \cdot 1_F + 1_F$. Then for every $n \ge 1$:

- $n \cdot 1_F > 0$ and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F > n \cdot 1_F$;
- the map $n \mapsto n \cdot 1_F$ is strictly increasing, hence injective, on $\{1, 2, 3, \dots\}$;
- $(m+n) \cdot 1_F = m \cdot 1_F + n \cdot 1_F$ and $(mn) \cdot 1_F = (m \cdot 1_F)(n \cdot 1_F)$ for all $m, n \ge 1$.

The **real numbers** are the quotient ring

$$\mathbb{R} := \mathcal{C} / \mathcal{N}$$

of the ring of Cauchy sequences ([[thm-cauchy-ring]]) by the ideal of null
sequences ([[lem-null-ideal]]). The class of $(a_n)$ is written
$[(a_n)]$. Each rational $q$ maps to the class $\hat q$ of the constant
sequence $(q, q, q, \dots)$.

An **ordered field** is a field $F$ ([[def-field]]) together with a subset
$P \subseteq F$, the set of **positive** elements (the *positive cone*),
satisfying:

- **(O1) Trichotomy.** For each $x \in F$, exactly one of the following holds:
  $x \in P$, or $x = 0$, or $-x \in P$.
- **(O2) Closure.** If $x, y \in P$ then $x + y \in P$ and $x \cdot y \in P$.

We write $x > 0$ for $x \in P$ (read "$x$ is positive"), and define the order by

$$a < b \;:\Longleftrightarrow\; b - a \in P, \qquad a \le b \;:\Longleftrightarrow\; a < b \text{ or } a = b.$$

Thus $a > b$ means $b < a$, and $a \ge b$ means $b \le a$. An element $x$ with
$-x \in P$ (equivalently $x < 0$) is called **negative**.

A real $x$ is **positive** when it has a representative $(a_n)$ together
with a rational $\delta > 0$ and an index $N$ such that $a_n > \delta$
for all $n \ge N$. Define

$$x \le y \iff x = y \;\text{ or }\; y - x \text{ is positive},$$

and $|x| = x$ if $x \ge 0$, $|x| = -x$ otherwise.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and let $x, y \in F$, with
$|x|$ the absolute value ([[def-abs-value]]). Then

$$|x| \ge 0; \quad |x| = 0 \iff x = 0; \quad -|x| \le x \le |x|; \quad |-x| = |x|; \quad |xy| = |x|\,|y|;$$

and, for every $c > 0$, one has $|x| < c \iff -c < x < c$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Assume the epsilon-delta condition and fix any stated sequence $x_n\to c$. For positive rational $\varepsilon$, [F1] gives a real $\delta>0$ such that $0<|x-c|<\delta$ implies $|f(x)-L|<\varepsilon$. By [F2], eventually $|x_n-c|<\delta$, and $x_n\ne c$ gives strict positivity. Thus eventually $|f(x_n)-L|<\varepsilon$, proving convergence in [F2]. No family of witnesses is selected: the sequence and one tolerance are fixed.

Conversely suppose the sequential condition holds but the epsilon-delta condition fails. Its negation yields one real $\varepsilon_0>0$ such that for every $\delta>0$ there exists $x\in A$ with $0<|x-c|<\delta$ and $|f(x)-L|\ge\varepsilon_0$. For each $n\in\mathbb N$, define $X_n=\{x\in A:0<|x-c|<1/(n+1),\ |f(x)-L|\ge\varepsilon_0\}$. Positivity of $n+1$ and the negated condition make every $X_n$ nonempty. These sets are a specified indexed family of subsets of the given set $A$.

Apply [A1] exactly once to obtain $x_n\in X_n$ for every $n$. Then $x_n\in A\setminus\{c\}$ and $|x_n-c|<1/(n+1)$. For every positive rational $q$, [F3] gives a threshold beyond which $1/(n+1)<q$, so $x_n\to c$ by [F2]. The sequential hypothesis therefore implies $f(x_n)\to L$.

Choose one rational $q$ with $0<q<\varepsilon_0$ by [F2]. Convergence in step 2.1 makes $|f(x_n)-L|<q<\varepsilon_0$ eventually, contradicting membership in $X_n$. Hence the epsilon-delta condition holds. The only countable selection was step 2.1; the forward implication and the two single rational choices require no choice axiom. The limit-point hypothesis and exclusion of $c$ are retained throughout.
